## Simple explanation

A hyperparameter is a setting chosen for a model or training process.
Examples include learning rate, batch size, and the number of layers.
The model's weights, in contrast, are usually learned from data.

## Technical explanation

Hyperparameters configure the hypothesis class, optimization procedure,
regularization, or data processing. They are selected before or around
training, often using validation data or an optimization procedure.
Some systems have hierarchical or learned hyperparameters, so the
distinction is based on their role in a particular training setup.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Hyperparameters affect performance, training stability, cost, and
deployment characteristics. Poor settings can waste compute or produce
models that underfit or overfit.

## How it works

Choose candidate settings, train models under those settings, and
compare them using a leakage-safe validation strategy. The selected
configuration is then retrained or finalized according to the
evaluation plan.

## Practical example

A training run may use a learning rate of 0.001 and a batch size of 64.
Those are hyperparameters, while the network weights are updated during
training.

## Common misconceptions

- Hyperparameters are not the same as model parameters learned by the
  optimizer.
- A hyperparameter that works for one dataset or architecture may not
  work for another.
- Tuning repeatedly on a test set leaks information into model
  selection.
